It sets itself apart from its parent [VolSDF Volume Rendering](2551-volsdf-volume-rendering.md) by explicitly deriving an "opaque density" $\rho(t)$ that ensures the weight function peaks exactly at the zero-level set of the SDF, and from its sibling [U-density Function](3695-u-density-function.md) by using signed distances and a specific derivative-based opacity formulation rather than unsigned distances and monotonic decay [S1, unofficial][S2].

The claim states that the method (NeuS, described in S1) differs from VolSDF by deriving an 'opaque density' to ensure the weight peaks at the SDF zero-level set, and differs from the U-density method (S2) by using signed distances and a derivative-based opacity formulation rather than unsigned distances and monotonic decay. Source S1 explicitly defines the 'opaque density' rho(t) derived from the SDF to create an unbiased weight function that peaks at the zero-level set. It contrasts this with naive solutions. Source S2 describes a 'naive UDF solution' that extends NeuS's weight to Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) and notes it suffers from bias. S1's derivation of rho(t) relies on the derivative of the SDF (signed), whereas the UDF approach in S2 uses the same weight structure but on unsigned distances, which S2 identifies as problematic (biased). Thus, the evidence supports the distinction regarding the use of signed distances and the specific derivative-based opaque density formulation to handle the zero-level set peak correctly, contrasting with the naive UDF application.
